title: Methodological Framework for Multi-Cell Posturography Enabling Unconstrained Foot Placement and Open-Platform Balance Assessment
content: Background/Objectives: Computer-assisted dynamic posturography is central to quan-tifying human postural control, yet many commercial systems often impose physical constraints such as small sensing surfaces that restrict larger foot sizes, high costs, and limited data interoperability arising from proprietary hardware and software. This study introduces a methodological framework and open-platform architecture (“OpenBal-ance”) intended to broaden access to mobile balance assessment by enabling uncon-strained foot placement. Methods: The proposed configuration uses an array of 16 dis-crete vertical-force load cells embedded in four mechanically decoupled sub-platforms intended to limit cross-talk and shear-force distortion. Biomechanical moment equations were implemented in a custom Python pipeline to compute a localized Center of Pressure (COP) for each sub-platform independently of weight shifts. A vector-based, ele-ment-wise data fusion maps these coordinates into a unified global coordinate system, alongside a time-averaged Weight Distribution Index (WDI). Results: A proof-of-concept trial using raw, unfiltered empirical data demonstrated that the cascading coordinate model produces a coherent global COP trajectory and per-quadrant load distribution, visualized with standard scientific Python libraries. The platform dimensions (355×460 mm) and sensor topography geometrically accommodate unconstrained external foot rotation and foot lengths corresponding to EU shoe sizes up to 55. Conclusions: The OpenBalance architecture indicates that a decentralized, cost-effective approach to pos-turography is feasible and can produce a continuous global COP from distributed load cells. Formal calibration and metrological validation against a reference standard remain necessary next steps. Future research should use this hardware-agnostic platform to develop structured, multi-sensory perturbation sequences to isolate discrete neu-ro-feedback loops in athletic and clinical cohorts.
